newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq says Ekeus meddling in government affairs.
newsitem.headline: Iraq says Ekeus meddling in government affairs.

text.p: The ruling Baath party newspaper al-Thawra on Wednesday accused Rolf Ekeus, chairman of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) on Iraq, of meddling in Baghdad's government affairs.
"He (Ekeus) has no right to give special opinion on the policies of the Iraqi government and on issues outside his mandate," the paper said in a front-page editorial.
It said UNSCOM, set up to oversee the scrapping of Iraq's weapons of mass destruction under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire, was purely a technical committee.
"This means that Iraqi government policies, stands and attitudes do not fall within Mr. Ekeus's prerogatives.
"But it seems that the former Swedish diplomat is determined to turn his technical tasks into political ones," Thawra said.
Remarks by Thawra came a day before Ekeus's next trip to Baghdad during which he is expected to hold both political and technical talks with Iraqi leaders.

Thawra's criticism fell short of demanding Ekeus's dismissal as UNSCOM chairman. Babel, the newspaper of President Saddam Hussein's eldest son Uday, on Tuesday called for his sacking. Another official newspaper last week accused him of "aggressive remarks."

Iraq and the United Nations are locked in dispute over the removal of some 100 wrecked missile engines for analysis to the United States. Iraq would like them to be examined in either Russia or France.
Iraq says it has destroyed all its banned missiles with ranges greater than 150 km (93 miles) but UNSCOM doubts the authenticity of the engines unearthed.
Thawra reiterated that Iraq had no more banned missiles left. It said Ekeus himself did not have evidence to prove his own suspicions.
The paper said Ekeus's persistence to keep the file of ballistic missiles open was giving the United States the opportunity to continue with its "blind enemity".
"We remind Ekeus that his commission bears moral as well as legal responsibilities...of the adverse impact of the embargo on Iraq and its citizens," Thawra said.

Sanctions imposed on Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait can be lifted only when Ekeus's commission decides that Iraq has scrapped all of its weapons of mass destruction including missiles with ranges greater than 150 km (93 miles).
